MPH Part 2: Dosage, side effects, contraindications

SitemapShow

66% of ADHD-HI and ADHD-C subtype children require moderate to high dosing.[1](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_1)[2](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_2)

The “last 10 mg” are particularly important in order to achieve an optimum effect.[3](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_3)

When adjusting the dosage, the increase in dosage should therefore not be stopped too early. Emotional depletion (“zombie”) is a sign of overdosing.

Adults require a significantly lower dosage, as the number of DAT (dopamine transporters) decreases with age. The number of DAT is halved in 50-year-olds compared to 10-year-olds; for adults, an initial dosage of max. 5 mg every 3 hours (immediate release) is recommended.

The half-life of MPH is:[4](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_4)

- for children approx. 2.5 hours
- for adults approx. 3.5 hours

## 6\. Dosage of MPH [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-6-dosage-of-mph "Permalink")

For details on the dosing of MPH and stimulants, see _[Dosing of medication for ADHD](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/232/dosing-of-medication-for-adhd)_

### 6.1. MPH not based on weight or age [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-61-mph-not-based-on-weight-or-age "Permalink")

Methylphenidate is not dosed across the board “according to body weight”. There are people with ADHD who manage with very low doses of MPH (3 to 5 mg every 3 hours). Others need the maximum recommended dose of 1 mg/kg body weight per day.

The maximum dose of 1 mg/kg body weight per day applies primarily to children. A comprehensive meta-analysis of 28 cohort studies on 5524 children and adolescents up to 18 years of age, in which the appropriate MPH dose was determined in stages, reported a range from 0.8 mg / kg / day to 1.8 mg / kg / day.[5](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_5) In persons with ADHD who tolerate MPH well and achieve only a moderate effect with lower doses, a dosage of more than 1 mg/kg/day can also be tested.[6](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_6)

One study reports a large variability in the optimal dose level (here using OROS-MPH):[7](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_7)

- 7.9 % with 18 mg
- 29.3 % with 36 mg
- 34.4 % with 54 mg
- 19.8 % with 72 mg
- 8.7 % with 90 mg

Another study found the optimal dose of sustained release MPH for children and adolescents:[8](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_8)

- 1.5 % with 10 mg
- 2.0 % with 15 mg
- 16.8 % with 20 mg
- 27.7 % with 30 mg
- 25.2 % with 40 mg
- 17.8 % with 50 mg
- 8.9 % with 60 mg

A clinical study comparing fixed and flexible dosing confirmed the benefits of an individually adjusted dose.[9](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_9)[10](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_10)

Blood levels of MPH vary greatly from individual to individual depending on the MPH dose taken.[11](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_11) The individual differences in effect are attributed to genetic differences in metabolization, among other things.[12](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_12)[13](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_13)

For adults (with a higher body weight), the required daily dose is usually significantly lower.

**lower dosage for adults**

Adults have far fewer dopamine transporters and therefore generally require less MPH than children. A dosage similar to that used in children can therefore already constitute an overdose in adults. Therefore, an even slower dosage in even lower steps (increase 2.5 mg to max. 5 mg immediate release / day, every 4 days) is recommended for adults. An overdose can cause the very symptoms that are supposed to be avoided, as the optimal dopamine level is already exceeded, causing very similar signal transmission problems to the low dopamine levels typical of ADHD. At a higher dosage (over 60 mg/day), individual neurologists report adaptation effects (not statistically proven).

Persons with ADHD-I presentation and even more ASD sufferers seem to require lower doses particularly frequently.

We know of several cases of affected adults who are optimally dosed with a single dose of 1.25 mg of immediate release MPH.

### 6.2. Daily coverage MPH [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-62-daily-coverage-mph "Permalink")

In any case, it is advisable to use MPH to cover the entire day, but not the late evening and night.

**Details**

Taking MPH only once (in the morning) for 3 (immediate release) or 6 hours (sustained release) means that the person with ADHD is at the mercy of their stress sensitivity again afterwards. MPH should be used with caution in the last few hours before going to bed. Most people react with sleep problems. For some, however, a quarter to half dose of stimulants enables them to fall asleep because it stops their thoughts from racing. It is possible that a low dose of immediate release stimulants could be helpful for people who already have low arousal. These are people who, for example, find it helpful to have a radio or television playing in the background to help them concentrate better. For others, listening to audio books helps them to fall asleep. People with a high arousal tend to need absolute silence in order to be able to concentrate.

For the different duration of action of the individual MPH drugs, see below under 7.

### 6.3. Dosage adjustment of methylphenidate [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-63-dosage-adjustment-of-methylphenidate "Permalink")

#### 6.3.1. Slow dosing in small steps [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-631-slow-dosing-in-small-steps "Permalink")

Slow and persistent dosing is important. In our opinion, the usual dosing practice in Germany is far too fast.

In principle, MPH should be dosed low at the start of the test and the dosage should only be increased slowly. Even if the optimal dosage were known, an immediate optimal dosage would possibly lead to excessive demands[14](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_14) and side effects.[15](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_15)

The dosage setting should start with 2.5 mg to a maximum of 5 mg/3-4 hours, which should only be increased to 3 x 5 = 15 mg/day within the first few days. Tests with higher starting dosages not only produced no better, but even worse efficacy results and at the same time resulted in a significantly higher discontinuation rate due to side effects.[15](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_15) Others recommend 2.5 to 5 mg twice daily, with a weekly increase of 2.5 to 5 mg.[6](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_6)[16](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_16)[14](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_14)[15](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_15)[17](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_17) Since such small dosing increments do not harm other people with ADHD (but on the contrary help to avoid dosing side effects), dosing increments in 2.5 mg steps (based on an immediate release single dose of MPH) should be the gold standard. So does Kühle. A large meta-analysis points in the same direction. Other sources recommend starting with 1-2 single doses of 5 mg and increasing the single dose weekly in 5 mg increments. For the reasons mentioned, we consider these dose increments to be too large.[18](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_18)[17](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_17)[19](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_19)[20](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_20)

For people with ADHD for whom even extremely small differences in dose are crucial, a pharmacy in Switzerland offers MPH drops. One drop contains 0.35 mg MPH. It is produced in batches and preserved using E216 and E218.[21](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_21) A person with ADHD reported that dissolving immediate release MPH in alcohol in such exact quantities that they could be measured out per drop showed a comparable result.

- Inform people with ADHD and observing third parties about the duration of action of the respective preparation and the expected rebound.
- We consider up-dosing by 2.5 mg per single dose every 5 to 7 days to be sensible. We now consider dosage increments of 5 mg / single dose, as we used to consider acceptable here, to be too high, because there is a relevant proportion of people with ADHD for whom 2.5 mg less means underdosing and 2.5 mg more means overdosing.[17](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_17) Even if this only represents a minority of people with ADHD, it would be malpractice to increase the dosage more quickly, as it is never possible to predict which group a person with ADHD belongs to. See also below: Gene variants influence MPH dosage.


The younger a person with ADHD is and the less they notice the MPH dose at all, the sooner the dosage increments can be increased.


In the course of adjustment, the dose is increased until the characteristics of an overdose are intensified with the next and subsequent dose increases. The dose that optimally reduces the symptoms without causing side effects can then be determined.


Unfortunately, there are known cases in which doctors have started discontinuation with single doses of 15 or 20 mg. We strongly advise against this.


Even if this were the right dosage for a few people with ADHD, the risk of suffering considerably more severe side effect problems in the first few weeks with such a high starting dosage would be significantly higher than with a slower adjustment.

#### 6.3.2. No caffeine with MPH dosage [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-632-no-caffeine-with-mph-dosage "Permalink")

Caffeine (theine is also caffeine), theobromine (dark cocoa) and other stimulants should be avoided at all costs when dosing. Caffeine, which was previously tolerated without any problems, can suddenly trigger internal tremors and other symptoms when taken simultaneously with stimulants, which can then be misinterpreted as a side effect of the medication. When new doses of stimulants are taken, caffeine can trigger a sensation similar to an overdose. Once the stimulants have been dosed, caffeine can be tried again. Sensations of discomfort can then be correctly attributed to caffeine.

#### 6.3.3. No nicotine withdrawal with MPH dosing [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-633-no-nicotine-withdrawal-with-mph-dosing "Permalink")

Nicotine withdrawal started at the same time as dosing can falsify the result. The need for cigarettes often decreases of its own accord after taking stimulants.

Similarly, restarting nicotine intake during stimulant dosing should be avoided.

#### 6.3.4. Age-related differences in dosage [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-634-age-related-differences-in-dosage "Permalink")

As adults have significantly fewer dopamine transporters than children (50-year-olds have only half as many as 10-year-olds,[22](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_22) a much lower dosage is indicated for adults than for children.

More on this at _⇒ [Dosing of medication for ADHD](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/232/dosing-of-medication-for-adhd)._

#### 6.3.5. Gene variants influence MPH levels [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-635-gene-variants-influence-mph-levels "Permalink")

A small proportion of people with ADHD require a significantly lower dosage of MPH.

The CES1 polymorphism Gly143Glu was found in 5.8% of people with ADHD and 4.1% of the population. No cases of CES1 Glu143Glu (homozygous) were found among 441 children.

CES1 Gly143Glu showed an unchanged reduction in inattention and hyperactivity-impulsivity on MPH.

Carriers of the CES1 143Glu variant (5.56 %) required almost 30 % lower doses of MPH to reduce symptoms.[23](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_23)

More on the influence of CES1 gene variants on the effect of MPH at _[Influences on the potency of MPH](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/186/mph-part-3-retardation)_ In the article _MPH Part 3: Degradation, potency_.

### 6.4. Side effects when discontinuing methylphenidate [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-64-side-effects-when-discontinuing-methylphenidate "Permalink")

In the first few days, taking the medicine can feel like snow has fallen - everything is wrapped in absorbent cotton. This (usually very pleasant) impression is due to the reduction in sensory overload and, like most side effects, disappears within a few days.

Others describe the initial effect with the impressive experience that for the first time in their lives their heads are calm and their thoughts are not racing.

Side effects such as headaches, sleep problems or other side effects rarely occur. Most side effects subside within the first few weeks after dosing. The risk of such side effects can be considerably reduced by very slow dosing (as described above).[15](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_15) A study with individually flexible dose adjustment reported a far below-average rate of 2.3% of dropouts due to side effects\[{ [Ginsberg Y, Arngrim T, Philipsen A, Gandhi P, Chen CW, Kumar V, Huss M (2014): Long-term (1 year) safety and efficacy of methylphenidate modified-release long-acting formulation (MPH-LA) in adults with attention-deficit hyperactivity disorder: a 26-week, flexible-dose, open-label extension to a 40-week, double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled core study. CNS Drugs. 2014 Oct;28(10):951-62. doi: 10.1007/s40263-014-0180-4. PMID: 25183661; PMCID: PMC4676085.](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4676085/)}} compared to studies with fixed doses, which in some cases amounted to 18.5 %.[13](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_13)\
\
To date, no known study in adults has explicitly prohibited the consumption of caffeine during dosing. Since caffeine drastically increases the rate of side effects during dosing, the rate of side effects should be significantly reduced if caffeine intake is consistently avoided compared to the study results.\
\
Headaches can sometimes be reduced or avoided by drinking enough and eating regularly (possibly glucose). As stimulants reduce the feeling of hunger, this can contribute to reduced fluid and food intake, which can also cause headaches.\
\
One study found that MPH did not cause sleep problems. This could differ from the results of other studies possibly because this study lasted a relatively long 16 weeks, so that the acclimatization side effects were no longer noticeable.[24](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_24) In contrast, a small study looking at just 14 days found reduced sleep duration and delayed sleep onset in children treated with sustained release MPH.[25](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_25)\
\
A higher increase in blood pressure at the first MPH dose correlated with better ADHD symptom reduction at 6 months.[26](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_26)\
\
### 6.5. Overdose symptoms with MPH [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-65-overdose-symptoms-with-mph "Permalink")\
\
With an appropriate dosage of MPH, the ability to concentrate increases and the internal pressure and any hyperactivity present decrease. If the latter increases again when the dosage is increased, this is a sign that the dosage is too high.\
\
Methylphenidate closes the stimulus filter (which is too wide open in people with ADHD). A typical reaction of people with ADHD with the right dosage is that they come to themselves, that they are more themselves.\
\
If the person with ADHD notices that MPH makes them jittery (although neither caffeine (theine is just another name for caffeine) nor theobromine (dark cocoa) is consumed), the dose should still be increased carefully at first. It has been observed several times that such side effects disappear again after a few days or at the next higher dose. If this shakiness persists, the dosage is too high. This also applies if the concentration becomes too high, i.e. the stimulus filter is restricted too far. Restricted emotionality (“zombie effects”) is a clear indication of an overdose.\
\
A study on monkeys concluded that low doses of MPH reduce impulsivity, while higher doses have a sedative effect.[27](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_27)\
\
This follows on from empirical experience that people with ADHD, especially children, can sometimes appear apathetic when taking MPH. Following this study, this indicates an overdose.\
\
Aripiprazole was able to reduce MPH overdose in rats.[28](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_28) This is all the more surprising as aripiprazole is a strong CES1 inhibitor and therefore reduces the degradation of MPH.[29](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_29)[4](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_4)\
\
### 6.6. Try different MPH medications even if MPH is effective, especially in the case of side effects / non-responding [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-66-try-different-mph-medications-even-if-mph-is-effective-especially-in-the-case-of-side-effects--non-responding "Permalink")\
\
Many people with ADHD report that they experience side effects with one MPH preparation that they do not experience with another MPH preparation. There are reports on this side that one MPH preparation (here: Medikinet) showed no effect, while another (here: Concerta) responded well.\
\
Other people with ADHD report that they experienced increased aggression with one preparation (here: Concerta), which did not occur with another MPH preparation (Medikinet or immediate release MPH).\
\
Others experience a stronger rebound effect with Medikinet (increase in agitation when the effect wears off) than with other MPH preparations.\
\
The various MPH preparations have very different release times, and MPH is embedded in different carriers depending on the manufacturer.\
\
In the case of an existing gluten intolerance, MPH embedded in wheat starch is naturally unsuitable. The same may apply to lactose intolerance.\
\
If a satisfactory effect is not achieved with all MPH preparations (the typical non-responder rate is just under 30%), medication with amphetamine drugs should always be given. As a result, a further 70 to 80 % of MPH non-responders can be satisfactorily medicated, so that the overall non-responder rate for MPH and AMP falls to below 10 %.\
\
If dysthymia or depression persists despite the satisfactory effect of MPH, a switch to amphetamine medication can also be considered, as these also have a mild serotonergic effect.\
\
Antidepressant effects were observed at MPH daily doses of 10 to 30 mg and at AMP daily doses of 5 to 60 mg.[6](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_6)\
\
### 6.7. Accompanying circumstances of recruitment and intake [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-67-accompanying-circumstances-of-recruitment-and-intake "Permalink")\
\
Some people with ADHD always need their MPH medication at exactly the same time.\
\
Care should be taken to ensure that the entire day is covered. However, the last doses of the day must be taken early enough so that there is no effect at bedtime.\
\
**Details**\
\
While on MPH, caffeine (coffee, black tea), theobromine (dark cocoa) and alcohol should be completely avoided, as these can intensify the effects of stimulants. Many people with ADHD report that MPH makes them much more sensitive to such stimulants. A jitteriness can therefore be triggered by caffeine, whereas the same amount of caffeine without MPH had no such effect. Like antidepressants, MPH often causes mild side effects (dry mouth etc.) in the first few days or weeks of taking it, which soon subside.\
\
To prevent or alleviate loss of appetite, it is recommended to take it with or after meals.\
\
### 6.8. Effect on those not affected [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-68-effect-on-those-not-affected "Permalink")\
\
MPH can also have an effect on people not suffering from ADHD. It can (in low doses) increase attention, just as mild stress increases cognitive performance by slightly increasing noradrenaline and dopamine in the PFC.\
\
A higher dosage in unaffected people (such as a low dosage in people who already have slightly elevated dopamine or noradrenaline levels) can cause DA and NE levels to become so elevated that ADHD symptoms are induced.\
\
In ADHD, the (tonic) dopamine level in the striatum is too low, which causes a number of ADHD symptoms. MPH increases the dopamine level in the striatum to the optimum level when dosed correctly. However, if the dopamine level is increased beyond the optimal level - by overdosing in people with ADHD or by taking MPH in healthy people - this triggers the same symptoms as in ADHD, because neurotransmitter communication only functions optimally at the correct neurotransmitter level.[30](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_30)\
\
Amphetamine drugs also have a positive effect (at low doses) in male mice that are not people with ADHD:[31](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_31)\
\
- Significant reduction in false alarms for males and females\
- Hit rate for females reduced\
- as a result, performance in the CPT (only) improved in males\
- Orientation and physical engagement with the task stimuli unimpaired\
\
The increase in dopamine in the dorsal striatum (but not in the nucleus accumbens) following amphetamine administration is higher in both male and female rats if they have previously been exposed to chronic uncontrollable stress. This could indicate a different dopaminergic response to stimulants (ADHD medication) in persons with ADHD and chronic stress.[32](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_32)\
\
Early childhood administration of MPH at both drug dose and overdose increased inflammatory markers, anxiety-like behavior and blood-brain barrier permeability in rats without ADHD, while in SHR (ADHD model animal) this only occurred at overdose, while drug dose improved not only behavior but also inflammation scores.[33](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_33)\
\
### 6.9. MPH in senior citizens [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-69-mph-in-senior-citizens "Permalink")\
\
There is no explicit restriction on the approval of methylphenidate for the elderly. The MPH product information contains a note that MPH should not be prescribed to older people. There is no such indication for lisdexamfetamine, despite equally inadequate data.\
\
Treatment with MPH at an older age should nevertheless be able to constitute an off-label prescription.[34](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_34)\
\
There are no indications that MPH would cause difficulties in old age.\
\
A small study reports good tolerability in older people with ADHD.[35](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_35)\
\
MPH is also used for age-related depression[36](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_36)\
\

## 9\. Quality of effect of methylphenidate [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-9-quality-of-effect-of-methylphenidate "Permalink")\
\
Methylphenidate is the first choice of medication for children. It combats the symptoms of ADHD significantly better than one year of behavioral therapy. Comparable effects are only achieved after 3 years of behavioral therapy.\
\
Since stimulants establish or increase the ability to learn and engage in therapy, it makes sense to initially work acutely with stimulants in order to create the basis for discontinuing them in parallel by means of behavioral therapy and/or neurofeedback.\
\
The mean Effect size of MPH for ADHD is between 0.9 and 1.3.\
\
For the effectiveness of individual medications and forms of treatment, see _⇒ [Effect size of different forms of treatment for ADHD](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/240/effect-size-of-different-forms-of-adhd-treatment)in the chapter⇒ [Treatment and therapy](https://www.adxs.org/de/page/179/behandlung-und-therapie)._\
\
MPH medication in combination with noradrenergic medication or zinc can further improve the effect. However, a cautious approach is recommended here. It is advisable to consult a doctor with experience in medication for ADHD.\
\
## 10\. Side effects of methylphenidate [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-10-side-effects-of-methylphenidate "Permalink")\
\
At an appropriate dosage, the effects of MPH give people with ADHD the feeling that they are much more themselves than before. If a person with ADHD feels that stimulants make them less themselves, this is a serious indication of incorrect dosing, misuse or misdiagnosis.\
\
Studies on the side effects of ADHD medications should always be checked to see which doses and which form of administration were used. Of course, stimulants cause side effects at certain doses. Anything that works can also have side effects. As the dose of the drug increases, these naturally also increase. The dose makes the poison.\
\
While doses of medication show slight benefits even in people who are not affected, higher doses are naturally harmful[51](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_51)\
\
,\
\
### 10.1. Side effects [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-101-side-effects "Permalink")\
\
#### 10.1.1. No serious side effects (- 9 %) [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1011-no-serious-side-effects---9- "Permalink")\
\
A Cochrane meta-analysis of MPH in children (mean age 9.7 years) found slightly less severe side effects with MPH than with placebo (OR = 0.91, k = 9, n = 1,532).[52](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_52)\
\
#### 10.1.2. Slightly increased risk of mild side effects (+ 29 %) [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1012-slightly-increased-risk-of-mild-side-effects--29- "Permalink")\
\
A Cochrane meta-analysis of MPH in children (mean age 9.7 years) found slightly more mild side effects with MPH than with placebo (OR = 1.29, k = 21, n = 3,132).[52](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_52)\
\
#### 10.1.3. No serious side effects with long-term use [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1013-no-serious-side-effects-with-long-term-use "Permalink")\
\
A systematic review found no serious side effects of long-term MPH use.[53](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_53) Long-term use did not cause any cardiovascular problems.[54](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_54)\
\
#### 10.1.4. Common side effects [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1014-common-side-effects "Permalink")\
\
“Common” side effects of MPH\
\
Common side effects of MPH can include\
\
(Common: occur in 1 to 10 %; 90 to 99 % of people taking MPH do not have these side effects)\
\
- Affect instability (mood swings)\
- Aggression\
- Agitation\
- Alopecia (hair loss)\
- Fear\
- Anorexia (weight loss, lack of weight gain)\
\
  - One comprehensive study found a slightly lower BMI in boys with ADHD on MPH.[55](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_55) In another study, the weight reduction due to MPH was only trended and not statistically significant.[56](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_56) A large meta-analysis of 38 cohort studies on 5524 participants up to 18 years of age found weight loss with an OR of 5.11 compared to placebo.[5](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_5)\
- abnormal behavior\
- Arrhythmia (cardiac arrhythmia; heart beats too quickly, too slowly or irregularly)\
- Arthralgia (joint pain)\
- Abdominal pain\
- Depression\
- Diarrhea\
- Dyskinesia (disorders of the movement sequence)\
- Vomiting\
- Skin rash\
- Cough\
- Hypertension (high blood pressure)\
\
  - A comprehensive study found no adverse effect of MPH on blood pressure in boys with ADHD.[57](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_57)\
- Stomach complaints\
- Dry mouth\
- Nasopharyngitis (inflammation of the nose/throat)\
- Palpitations (subjective feeling that the heart is beating too fast / too strongly / irregularly)\
- Pruritus (itching)\
- psychomotor hyperactivity\
\
  - frequent signs of overdose\
- Pyrexia (fever)\
- Throat and larynx pain\
- Irritability\
- Sleep problems\
\
  - Problems falling asleep\
\
    - Advice on taking too late in the day\
  - Daytime tiredness\
- Dizziness\
- Tachycardia (heart rate over 100 beats / minute)\
- Nausea\
- Urticaria (hives)\
- Growth retardation with prolonged use in children.\
\
Most of the side effects mentioned are non-specific and do not play a major role in practice[58](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_58)\
\
A comparison of the side effects with the package insert for aspirin or SSRI is recommended for classification.\
\
A large meta-analysis of 38 cohort studies involving 5524 participants up to 18 years of age found the most common side effects to be sleep problems (OR 4.66), weight loss (OR 5.11), abdominal pain (OR 1.9) and headaches (in 14% of MPH takers) compared to placebo.[5](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_5) Sleep problems are often caused by dosing too late in the day, especially when starting dosing. Very slow dosing can help to avoid side effects. Most of these side effects disappear within the first few weeks.\
\
For some people with ADHD, the administration of a small immediate release dose (1/4 to 1/2 of a single daily dose) helps them to fall asleep.[6](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_6)\
\
A study that lasted 16 weeks found that MPH did not cause sleep problems.[24](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_24) In contrast, a small study that looked at only 14 days found reduced sleep duration and delayed falling asleep in children treated with sustained release MPH.[25](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_25) This is consistent with the experience that sleep problems are possible with MPH, but are usually only a side effect of dosing. We conclude that in case of sleep problems due to MPH during the first weeks, it might be helpful to shorten the daytime coverage. Regardless of this, slow dosing in increments of max. 2.5 mg / single dose of immediate release MPH is always recommended.\
\
One study reported a statistically significant increase in intraocular pressure of only the left eye due to MPH in ADHD. A change in the thickness of the macular, retinal nerve fiber layer (RNFL) or ganglion cell layer (GCL) was not reported.[59](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_59)\
\
Most side effects only occur shortly after starting the medication and regularly disappear within the first four weeks. The short-lived feeling of a dry / furry tongue shortly after taking the medication may last longer, but it goes away quite reliably at some point.\
\
Tic disorders are observed with overdoses. If people with ADHD have the feeling for months that the world is moving away or that life is becoming monotonous, this is also a clear indication of overdose.\
\
#### 10.1.5. Side effects primarily with comorbid anxiety or other comorbidities [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1015-side-effects-primarily-with-comorbid-anxiety-or-other-comorbidities "Permalink")\
\
Several studies have found that adverse reactions to stimulants occur primarily in people with ADHD with higher anxiety levels and faster reaction times or pre-existing comorbidities.[60](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_60)[61](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_61)\
\
No correlation with EEG values was found.[61](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_61)\
\
#### 10.1.6. Gene variants with increased risk of MPH side effects [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1016-gene-variants-with-increased-risk-of-mph-side-effects "Permalink")\
\

- Buccal-lingual movements: 1065G\
- Diastolic blood pressure: ADRA2A Mspl C/C-GC\

- Irritability: SNAP25 T1065G\
- Plucking: DRD4 _7/DRD4_ 4\
- social withdrawal: DRD4 _7/DRD4_ 4\
- somatic complaints: DAT1\*10/10\
- Tics: 5-HTTLRP _S/L_ L/L and SNAP25 T1065G\
- Sadness: CES1\*rsl12443580\
- vegetative symptoms: 5-HTTLPR\
\
### 10.2. Growth in length delayed for a short time [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-102-growth-in-length-delayed-for-a-short-time "Permalink")\
\
Several comprehensive studies have found no persistent impairment of length growth in boys with ADHD by MPH.[55](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_55)\
\
A temporary impairment of longitudinal growth in the first year of MPH treatment was recovered in the second year.[56](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_56) Temporary impairment of longitudinal growth is common in ADHD in childhood and is regularly recovered in adolescence. This is apparently not a specific effect of methylphenidate.[63](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_63) Another study found a 4-fold increased risk of reduced length growth and weight gain in children with ADHD at ages 8 and 10. The length of stimulant treatment increased this risk.[64](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_64)\
\
### 10.3. Parkinson’s / Tremor in old age [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-103-parkinsons--tremor-in-old-age "Permalink")\
\
A very comprehensive study analyzed the probability of disorders from the Parkinson’s disease spectrum (simple tremor to Parkinson’s disease) in people with ADHD with and without stimulant use over decades of their lifetime.[65](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_65)\
\
The results of the study are extremely interesting:\
\
1. ADHD increases the lifetime likelihood of Parkinson’s (-like) Disorder by 2.4 times\
2. Parkinson’s (-like) disorders are even more likely if the persons with ADHD had taken stimulants (6-fold)\
3. Parkinson’s (-like) disorders are 8 times more common in persons with ADHD who were given methylphenidate than in non-affected persons\
\
It should be noted:\
\
1. The result contradicts a later long-term study (see below).\
2. The correlation is correct\
3. Causality is questionable\
\
\
Is Parkinson’s more likely in stimulant users or in more severe ADHD, which is more commonly treated with stimulants?\
\
\
The study design does not allow a statement on this. Other studies will be needed for this.\
4. The increased risk of comorbidity in ADHD is not limited to Parkinson’s.\
\
\
The probability of early death is drastically increased with untreated ADHD: from 0.8% for people without ADHD to 2.3% for people with ADHD, i.e. plus 1.5 percentage points\
\
The absolute figures are more revealing.\
\
Disorder of the basal ganglia or cerebellum (a disorder related to Parkinson’s (tremor) or Parkinson’s disease) got\
\
- 56 of 24,792 non-ADHD persons with ADHD = 0.23 %\
  - Of which 26 = 0.1 % with less than 50 years\
  - Of which 19 = 0.08 % developed Parkinson’s disease\
- 104 of 26,809 persons with ADHD who were not known to be receiving stimulants = 0.39 %\
  - Of which 69 = 0.26 % with less than 50 years of age\
  - Of which 38 = 0.14 % developed Parkinson’s disease\
- 62 of 4960 persons with ADHD who were known to be receiving stimulants = 1.25 %\
  - Of which 42 = 0.85 % with less than 50 years\
  - Of which 19 = 0.38 % developed Parkinson’s disease\
\
60% of stimulant users had taken amphetamines and 40% had taken methylphenidate. If the risk is 6-fold higher for all stimulant users and 8-fold higher for MPH, which was taken by only 40%, it must therefore be significantly lower than 4-fold for amphetamine drugs.\
\
This means that the risk of Parkinson’s (related) Disorder could be estimated to be\
\
- 1 % for ADHD, treated with amphetamine medication\
- 2 % for ADHD, treated with methylphenidate\
\
One could also - just as correctly - formulate this:\
\
The risk of developing a Parkinson’s (related) Disorder within 20 years is increased by 0.16 percentage points in people who have ADHD (0.16% more people develop a Parkinson’s (related) Disorder if they have ADHD than if they do not). If amphetamine medication is taken, the increase is 1 percentage point higher compared to those who are not affected; if methylphenidate is prescribed, the risk is increased by 2 percentage points.\
\
If you convert that to 100,000 people:\
\
- 1.5% of 100,000 is 1,500 additional premature deaths due to ADHD\
- 1% of 100,000 is 1,000 additional people with ADHD (from a simple tremor to Parkinson’s) on amphetamine medication for ADHD (without knowing whether this is due to the severity of the ADHD or the AMP).\
- 2% of 100,000 is 2,000 additional people with ADHD (from a simple tremor to Parkinson’s) on methylphenidate for ADHD (without knowing whether this is due to the severity of the ADHD or the MPH).\
\
But if someone who now has ADHD has a choice,\
\
- With untreated ADHD tripled the risk of early death from 0.8% to 2.3% (absolute: plus 1.5 percentage points)\
- What medication can largely remedy\
- Or to accept an increased risk of Parkinson’s type disorders (from a simple tremor to Parkinson’s disease) by a factor of three to eight, but in absolute terms only by 1 to 2 percentage points,\
\
most people would prefer to have a trembling hand when alive than a steady one when dead.\
\
It also follows that if ADHD is treatable with amphetamine medications, these should be preferred over MPH.\
\
Against this background, the wording of the study results sounds somewhat tendentious or attention-seeking.\
\
The study design would be perfect to show how much higher mortality is with medication. However, this - much more important - question is not answered, even though this data should have really jumped out at the authors. Similarly, no differentiation is made between the fact that the risk was only half as high with amphetamine medication as with methylphenidate, but only the higher figure for methylphenidate was mentioned.\
\
The increase in the risk of Parkinson’s type disorders (from a simple tremor to Parkinson’s disease) due to chronic overdose of MPH could result from an increased production of quinones and a decrease in glutathione (GSH, γ-L-glutamyl-L-cysteinylglycine).[66](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_66) Chronic administration of 10 mg MPH / kg (approximately 10 times the maximum therapeutic amount in humans) promoted a loss of dopaminergic cells in the substantia nigra.[67](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_67) A loss of dopaminergic cells could explain Parkinson’s symptoms. This also indicates that high doses of MPH should be avoided if possible.\
\
A German study found no evidence of a correlation between Parkinson’s and the use of psychostimulants such as methylphenidate in childhood.[68](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_68)\
\
Another long-term study found that stimulant prescriptions for ADHD reduced the risk of Parkinson’s disease by 60%[69](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_69)\
\
### 10.4. Slightly increased risk of psychosis at best [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-104-slightly-increased-risk-of-psychosis-at-best "Permalink")\
\
According to a very large study, the risk of developing psychosis is lower for people with ADHD taking MPH (0.10%) than for those treated with amphetamine medication (0.21%).[70](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_70) Another study found a similar ratio.[71](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_71)\
\
While people with ADHD treated with stimulants have 2.4 cases of psychosis per 1000 person-years (0.24%), the figure for the population as a whole is 0.0214%[72](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_72)\
\
The studies do not allow any conclusion to be drawn as to whether the increase in the prevalence of psychosis is due to the existence of ADHD or to the administration of stimulants.\
\
Another study found an 8-fold risk for people with ADHD when taking ADHD medication (0.34% vs. 0.048%).[73](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_73) As this does not compare people with ADHD with and without medication, but people with ADHD with medication against the general population, it is not possible to draw any reliable conclusions about the contribution of ADHD medication. The absolute risk of a first-time hospitalization for psychosis or mania when starting medication was drug-dependent:\
\
- Atomoxetine: 0.60 % (highest)\
- Amphetamine drugs: 0.33 %\
- Methylphenidate: 0.19 %\
\
Another large cohort study, which generally found a significantly increased risk of psychosis with ADHD, indicates that stimulants increase the risk slightly at best. Stimulants further increased this risk very slightly (6%), while the increase of 15% for non-stimulants was almost three times as high as for stimulants.[74](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_74) Another large study based on the Swedish health register with 23,898 adolescents and young adults with ADHD compared the risk of psychosis before and after MPH administration and found only a non-significant increase of 4% in the risk of psychosis with methylphenidate.[75](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_75) If so, high doses of MPH appear to increase the risk of psychosis.[76](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_76)\
\
The benefits of treating ADHD (reduction in premature mortality, reduction in lifetime risk of depression and anxiety disorders, reduction in risk of addiction, etc.) are likely to significantly outweigh the potential risk.\
\
More on the risks of (untreated) ADHD at _⇒ [Consequences of ADHD](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/52/consequences-of-adhd)_.\
\
### 10.5. Increased risk of anorexia [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-105-increased-risk-of-anorexia "Permalink")\
\
Treatment with MPH increases the risk of anorexia by 4.66 times.[77](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_77)\
\
Treatment with stimulants should therefore be avoided in people with ADHD with anorexia tendencies.\
\
In an RCT, MPH significantly reduced the “hunger neuropeptide” NPY, which regulates food intake and the reduction of anxiety and stress, by 21%.[78](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_78)\
\
### 10.6. Seizure threshold, EEG abnormalities [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-106-seizure-threshold-eeg-abnormalities "Permalink")\
\
Methylphenidate is said to be able to lower the seizure threshold. This applies to patients with an existing history of seizures (e.g. epileptics) as well as patients with abnormalities in the EEG without previous seizures. In rare cases, MPH can trigger seizures even without the aforementioned previous risks.\
\
A study with n = 478 subjects found EEG abnormalities in 273 (52.8 %). Children with and without EEG abnormalities showed similar patterns of MPH use (initial use, positive reaction and maintenance of MPH use). A follow-up of n = 39 persons with ADHD with EEG abnormalities showed no increase in seizures after 3 years of MPH use. Only 3 children with drug-resistant epilepsy had seizures, although their frequency had not increased. In the case of comorbid epilepsy and EEG abnormalities, the risk of seizures was unchanged when MPH was taken.[79](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_79)\
\
If the frequency of seizures increases or if new seizures occur, methylphenidate should be discontinued.[80](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_80)\
\
### 10.7. Stimulation of existing anxiety disorders, depression, aggression [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-107-stimulation-of-existing-anxiety-disorders-depression-aggression "Permalink")\
\
Comorbid anxiety disorders, depression and aggression can be exacerbated by stimulants, as anxiety and moods are regulated by the dopaminergic activity of the ventromedial PFC in conjunction with the limbic system. In these cases, noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors or α2A-adrenoceptor agonists are recommended instead.[81](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_81)\
\
One (quite small) study found no short-term change in state anxiety with a single dose of MPH, but did find evidence of a possible long-term worsening.[82](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_82)\
\
### 10.8. MPH and mania risk in Bipolar Disorder [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-108-mph-and-mania-risk-in-bipolar-disorder "Permalink")\
\
One study found that MPH was not associated with an increased risk of mania in patients with bipolar Disorder. After MPH treatment, mania decreased by 50 %. Depressive episodes and psychiatric admissions also decreased.[83](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_83)\
\
### 10.9. MPH increases histamine [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-109-mph-increases-histamine "Permalink")\
\
MPH increases histamine,[84](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_84) as do all other known ADHD medications:\
\
- Atomoxetine\
- Amphetamine\
- Modafinil\
- Nicotine\
- Caffeine\
\
This is why people with histamine intolerance often have problems due to taking ADHD medication.\
\
A person with ADHD with histamine intolerance reported that she could not tolerate AMP and sustained release MPH at all, but could tolerate immediate release MPH in small doses.\
\
### 10.10. Rebound [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1010-rebound "Permalink")\
\
A rebound is a short-term increase in symptoms that are actually reduced by MPH at the end of the medication’s effective period. If a dose of MPH works for around 3 hours, ADHD symptoms may increase for around 20 to 30 minutes at the end of the 3 hours or immediately afterwards.\
\
Rebound is reported more frequently and more clearly with immediate release MPH than with sustained release MPH.[85](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_85)\
\
We assume that a rebound is caused by too rapid a decline in dopamine/noradrenaline levels. A rebound seems to occur less frequently with drugs that show a very slow decline in effect.\
\
A rebound can be avoided by taking the follow-up dose in good time so that no drug-free period remains.\
\
For the last daily dose, the rebound should be mitigated or avoided by taking a much smaller dose than the usual single dose at the time when the subsequent dose would otherwise be taken.\
\
### 10.11. MPH and narcosis / anesthesia [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1011-mph-and-narcosis--anesthesia "Permalink")\
\
In the case of surgery, in addition to the sometimes significantly increased (drug) sensitivity of people with ADHD, the question of cross-effects of ADHD drugs with anesthetics must also be considered.\
\
A double-blind study from 1980 found no change in postoperative pain with MPH. Methylphenidate shortened postoperative sedation by up to 30 minutes and improved respiratory function by up to 180 minutes with halothane anesthesia.[86](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_86) Halothane is no longer used today.\
\
One case study reports a reduced response to sedatives and increased side effects due to MPH.[87](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_87)\
\
One study reports a correlation between attention problems and postoperative delirium.[88](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_88)\
\
### 10.12. Other side effects of MPH [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1012-other-side-effects-of-mph "Permalink")\
\
Individual cases of trichotillomania (pulling out hair) have been reported.[89](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_89) Trichotillomania is a specific form of impulse control disorder.\
\
One study reported muscle pain and stiffness as a possible side effect of MPH.[90](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_90)\
\
One study reported a doubled rate of testosterone deficiency in adult persons with ADHD after 5 years of stimulant use (1.2%) compared to persons with ADHD without stimulant use (0.67%) or non-stimulant use (0.68%).[91](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_91)\
\
### 10.13. No increased cardiovascular risks [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1013-no-increased-cardiovascular-risks "Permalink")\
\
The hypothesis that methylphenidate would cause increased heart problems was not confirmed.[92](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_92) Changes in EEG values were not found.[61](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_61) A meta-analysis found slightly increased values below statistical significance.[93](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_93)\
\
An initial study with n = 564 people with ADHD, which had suspected an increased cardiac death rate in children taking MPH, was refuted by a large number of other studies, including a large study with n = 241,417 with MPH-medicated children.[94](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_94) A very large study found no increased risk of serious cardiovascular events such as stroke, heart attack or cardiac arrhythmia for MPH among 2,566,995 children.[95](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_95) A third large registry study with n = 224,732 people also found no increased long-term cardiovascular risks due to MPH. The risk rates were even reduced by 15 %[96](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_96)\
\
There are also studies that even confirm a reduced risk of cardiac death under MPH, which could be explained by the medical care provided to people with ADHD.\
\
Several studies found no significant change in heart rate, QRS, QT, QTc and QTd interval in ECGs due to MPH.\
\
The Tp-Te intervals and Tp-Te/QTc ratios were slightly increased after treatment with MPH, but within normal values.[97](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_97) Children with ADHD showed significantly prolonged P-wave dispersion, TpTe interval, TpTe dispersion, and TpTe/QT and TpTe/QTc ratios. In addition, almost half of the patients had QTc values of 460 ms or more. These parameters were not associated with either MPH dose or treatment duration.[98](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_98) QTc interval and fQRS-T angle were significantly higher in both drug-naïve and medicated people with ADHD than in the healthy control group. However, QTc interval and fQRS-T angle were unchanged between drug-naïve and medicated persons with ADHD. Both QTc interval and fQRS-T angle correlated with the severity of ADHD symptoms.[99](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_99)\
\
One study found no increased risk of cardiac arrhythmias for methylphenidate. However, an increased risk of cardiac arrhythmia was found for atomoxetine for 7 days after the first exposure to atomoxetine (aIRR 6.22) and for subsequent exposure (aIRR 3.23).[100](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_100)\
\
A study over 14 years found a 4% increase in the risk of cardiovascular problems per year of taking stimulants (methylphenidate, amphetamines) and, to a lesser extent, the non-stimulant atomoxetine.[101](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_101)\
\
A cohort study of n = 252,382 with a mean age of 20 years found a posterior probability of at least 10% increased risk of cardiovascular events of 70% in people receiving MPH compared to 49% in matched controls. There was no difference in risk between people with and without a history of cardiovascular disease.[102](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_102)\
\
Long-term use did not cause any cardiovascular problems.[103](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_103)\
\
In adults, cardiovascular problems are said to be possible due to MPH.[104](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_104)\
\
### 10.14. Liver damage not known [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1014-liver-damage-not-known "Permalink")\
\
No increased reports of liver damage are known with MPH.[105](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_105) However, liver values should always be monitored when discontinuing ADHD medication.\
\
### 10.15. No negative long-term effects of MPH [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1015-no-negative-long-term-effects-of-mph "Permalink")\
\
The reports known to us to date on the harmful effects of long-term use of MPH are all based on massive overdoses. Such studies are common and useful for testing the limits of an active ingredient’s tolerability. However, they say nothing about the dangers of long-term use in normal doses.\
\
To put this into perspective: humans need 30 to 40 ml of water per kg per day (2 to 3 liters). however, 3 liters of water at once or 5 liters of water per day can already have a lethal effect. This means that even doubling the amount of water given to humans can have fatal effects.\
\
A large-scale long-term study of MPH over 2 years in children with ADHD found in the MPH group:[106](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_106)\
\
- no significant impairment of growth\
- slight weight loss in the first 6 months, which then subsided\
- no change in relation to psychosis, depression, dyskinesia, tics\
- slightly elevated blood pressure and pulse\
- preventive effect in relation to addiction and suicide\
\
  - significantly increased nicotine and marijuana use in the non-MPH group\
  - significantly increased suicidal tendencies in the non-MPH group\
\
A population-based cohort study with data from Danish registries of patients who had taken either Medikinet® MR or Concerta® continuously for a prolonged period (i.e. ≥ 12 months) between 1995 and 2018 found:[107](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_107)\
\
- no cases of cerebral arteritis\
- no cases of priapism\
- no case of sudden death with Medikinet® MR\
- no statistically significant risk differences between Medikinet® MR and Concerta®\
\
A study in primates found no change in brain parameters 6 months after the end of 12 years of long-term administration of MPH.[108](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_108)\
\
A study in adult rats found damage to the morphology and function of the cerebellum after long-term administration of 15 to 20 times the usual daily dose.[109](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_109) This is as expected at such doses.\
\
A study on rats that received 5 mg/kg/day, five times the maximum daily dose normally given to humans during puberty, found that sperm quality was impaired in the adult animals.[110](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_110) Moreover, these were Wistar rats, i.e. rats that do not have a dopamine deficiency.\
\
A study on Balb/c mice (an animal model for ASA), which also did not show a dopamine deficit but rather an excess of dopamine[111](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_111), found an impairment of sperm quality by MPH. This study also speculated about a toxicity of MPH due to a weight loss of the animals to 20 mg/kg and 40 mg/kg MPH, which is similar to a drug dose.[112](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_112) It is well known that stimulants reduce appetite. That dopamine-increasing active ingredients are detrimental in animals that do not have reduced dopamine levels is not surprising, but to be expected.\
\
No statistically significant difference in sperm count was found in people with ADHD after taking methylphenidate, but there was a significant difference in sperm motility and abnormality[113](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_113)\
\
In one study, monkeys were given 2.5 mg/kg or 12.5 mg/kg MPH twice daily. 12.5 mg/kg twice daily is around 25 times the maximum dose usually recommended for humans and, in our view, represents a drug dose rather than a medication dose.\
\
Apart from a temporary reduction in motivation after the end of MPH administration (again, only with the “drug dose”), no negative effects were found [114](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_114)\
\
At twice 12.5 mg/kg/day, there was also a significant deterioration in cognitive performance, as would be expected with such an overdose.[115](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_115)\
\
### 10.16. Reduced risk of stress fractures [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1016-reduced-risk-of-stress-fractures "Permalink")\
\
MPH use by persons with ADHD reduced the risk of stress fractures compared to non-affected people (without MPH use).[116](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_116)\
\
### 10.17. Reduced risk of type 2 diabetes [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1017-reduced-risk-of-type-2-diabetes "Permalink")\
\
Methylphenidate reduced the risk of type 2 diabetes by 20% in the first 3 years of use.[117](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_117) Long-term use of atomoxetine for more than 3 years increased the risk by 44%. Lisdexamfetamine had no effect.\
\
## 11\. Interactions and contraindications [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-11-interactions-and-contraindications "Permalink")\
\
As with any medication, there are also contraindications for MPH.\
\
Taking it without prior medical consultation is risky!\
\
Methylphenidate is metabolized independently of the cytochrome P450 system, so that there is only a very low potential for pharmacokinetic interactions.[80](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_80)\
\
### 11.1. Interactions of methylphenidate with other medications [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-111-interactions-of-methylphenidate-with-other-medications "Permalink")\
\
#### 11.1.1. Enhanced effect of other drugs / substances due to MPH [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1111-enhanced-effect-of-other-drugs--substances-due-to-mph "Permalink")\
\
- Caffeine can have a more intensive effect\
\
\
Caffeine should be strictly avoided, especially when taking stimulants (e.g. MPH). Stimulants often cause caffeine in doses that were previously tolerated without any problems to trigger an inner tremor. This can be wrongly interpreted as a (side) effect of the stimulants.\
\
\
A very high dose of caffeine (tens of times above drug level) over several days reduced the efficacy of MPH in rats, and vice versa. This confirms that MPH and caffeine have common,[118](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_118)[119](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_119) but not identical[120](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_120) mechanisms of action.\
\
- Alcohol\
\
\
A comprehensive meta-analysis found little evidence that ADHD medication in combination with alcohol or other drugs would have any particular negative effects.[121](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_121)\
  - Taken together with MPH, alcohol can have a more intensive effect\
  - Alcohol taken together with MPH can increase MPH levels[122](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_122)\
- All sympathomimetics[123](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_123) can be strengthened by MPH.\
\
\

#### 11.1.3. Changes in the effect of MPH due to other medications [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-1113-changes-in-the-effect-of-mph-due-to-other-medications "Permalink")\
\
An increased gastric pH above 5.5 can accelerate / increase the release of the sustained release components of Medikinet adult. However, the release of methylphenidate from Ritalin adult is pH-independent. Nevertheless, a reduction in absorption is possible with Ritalin adult due to antacids.[80](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_80)\
\
The stomach pH value can be increased by:\
\
- Proton pump inhibitors, e.g.\
\
  - Pantoprazole\
  - Omeprazole\
- H2 antagonists (although less likely), e.g.\
\
  - Ranitidine\
  - Famotidine\
- Antacids\
\
Chronic oral MPH alone produced a tendency in the striatum of rats to[130](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_130)\
\
- Increased dynorphin expression\
- Increased substance P expression\
- Unchanged enkephalin expression.\
\
Oral fluoxetine alone did not change the expression of these genes.\
\
MPH and fluoxetine together caused\
\
- Strongly increased dynorphin expression\
- Strongly increased substance P expression\
- Increased enkephalin expression\
\
Oxytocin potentiates MPH-induced stimulation of tonic (extracellular) dopamine firing, probably by modulating dopamine receptor signaling pathways. Oxytocin did not affect MPH-induced dopamine reuptake or MPH-induced phasic dopamine firing.[131](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_131)\
\
CBD (cannabidiol) only marginally affected MPH levels and AUC, although CBD is a CES1 inhibitor[132](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_132)\
\

### 11.2. MPH and blood pressure [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-112-mph-and-blood-pressure "Permalink")\
\
Methylphenidate can increase blood pressure in children.\
\
In children with ADHD, blood plasma levels of nitric oxide appear to be increased and asymmetric dimethylarginine (ADMA) decreased. ADMA inhibits the blood pressure-increasing effect of nitric oxide. When MPH was taken, the nitric oxide plasma values increased further. This could possibly be due to a reduced inhibition of nitric oxide by ADMA during MPH administration and could be a cause of the blood pressure-increasing effect of MPH.[104](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_104)\
\
In contrast, a comprehensive study found no adverse effect of MPH on blood pressure in boys with ADHD.[57](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_57)\
\
Patients at risk of high blood pressure should therefore weigh up the extent to which the possible risk of a drug-induced increase in blood pressure outweighs the possible benefit of reduced blood pressure due to reduced sensitivity to stress.\
\
A higher increase in blood pressure when first taking methylphenidate indicated a greater ADHD symptom reduction after 6 months.[26](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_26)\
\
### 11.3. MPH intake during pregnancy [¶](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications\#content-113-mph-intake-during-pregnancy "Permalink")\
\
Studies on the use of MPH during pregnancy found the following with regard to the offspring\
\
- Weight\
\
  - unchanged[133](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_133)[134](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_134)\
  - slightly reduced[135](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_135)\
- Risks of pre-eclampsia, placental abruption or premature birth with stimulant use (AMP or MPH) during pregnancy, although these were so low that the authors did not recommend discontinuing stimulant use during pregnancy.[135](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_135) Atomoxetine did not show these slight increases in risk.\
- Risk of miscarriage due to stimulants during pregnancy\
\
  - not statistically significantly changed by methylphenidate and atomoxetine (meta-analysis, k = 10, n = 16,621,481)[136](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_136)\
  - doubled[137](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_137)\
- Malformations\
\
  - very small increase (not relevant)[138](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_138)\
  - no increased risk.[139](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_139)\
  - slightly increased (meta-analysis, k = 4) in relation to malformations and cardiac malformations with MPH intake in early pregnancy[140](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_140)\
  - not statistically significantly increased by methylphenidate and atomoxetine (+ 14 %) (meta-analysis, k = 10, n = 16,621,481)[136](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_136)\
- ADHDsymptoms\
\
\
  - increased in study on mice\
  - reduced expression of the D2 receptor and dopamine transporter genes, which are common in ADHD, at 2.5 to 15 times the usual maximum drug level[141](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_141) This is plausibly consistent with the model of brain development disorders caused by a lack of dopamine (e.g. genetically inherited or due to chronic stress) or an excess of dopamine (e.g. due to stimulant administration in unaffected individuals). More on this at _⇒ [Brain development disorder and ADHD](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/68/brain-development-disorder-and-adhd)_ In the chapter _⇒ [Development](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/54/development-of-adhd-introduction)._\
  - no increased risk of ADHD or other neuronal developmental disorders due to MPH or AMP use during pregnancy. The increased ADHD risk initially found was due to the mothers’ ADHD on closer examination.[142](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_142)\
- neurological developmental disorders\
\
  - Risk unchanged (Swedish cohort study, n = 861,650 children of n = 572,731 mothers from 2008-2017)[143](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_143)\
\

Caution is advised when using methylphenidate for:[80](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_80)\

- Hyperthyroidism\
- Thyrotoxicosis\
- Severe depression\

\
  - Schizophrenia\
  - Mania\
  - Bipolar Disorder Type I\
- Cardiomyopathies\
\

- Asthma[144](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_144)\
- Interstitial pneumonia or fibrosis[144](https://www.adxs.org/en/page/185/mph-part-2-dosage-side-effects-contraindications#fn_144)\
